_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: Structs and the dot operator
rungs.builds: Variables and types (Phase 2): int and float variables. Arrays: many values, one name (Phase 3): many boxes of the same type.
rungs.why: A player in your game has a position and health, and maybe more. Without a struct you’d carry loose variables around and hope you never mix up whose x is whose. A struct bundles them into one thing you can name, copy and pass around.

parts: One name for a bundle

A struct groups a few values that belong together under one name. Each value is a field, and the fields can have different types: a Player might have two floats for its position and an int for its health. typedef gives the new type a one-word name, so you can write Player hero; the way you'd write int lives;. The dot then picks one field: hero.health behaves exactly like an int variable.
Giving it starting values

A struct made with no starting values is garbage in every field, like any local variable. There are three ways to fill it as you make it:

  • Player hero = {0}; sets every field to zero, the same rule you used for arrays.
  • Player hero = {2.5f, 0.0f, 100}; fills the fields in the order they're declared. It breaks quietly if someone reorders the fields later.
  • Player hero = {.health = 100, .x = 2.5f}; names each field. Order doesn't matter, and any field you leave out becomes 0. These are designated initialisers, and they're the clearest of the three.
Field names belong to the struct

A field name only means something after a dot. You can have a plain variable called health next to hero.health, and a Player and an Enemy can both have an x. They never clash, because the compiler always knows which struct you're reaching into.
Two ways to name the type

Without typedef, the name after struct is a tag, and you have to repeat the word struct every time:

struct Player {
    float x;
    int health;
};

struct Player hero;

Plenty of code you'll read does both at once: typedef struct Player { ... } Player;. Now struct Player and Player mean the same type. This course leaves the tag out unless it's needed.
A struct inside a struct

A field can be another struct. Position is a pair of numbers you'll use everywhere, so give it its own type and put it inside Player:

typedef struct { float x; float y; } Vec2;
typedef struct { Vec2 pos; int health; } Player;

Read hero.pos.x = 3.0f; left to right: hero, then its pos, then that Vec2's x. Vec2 has to be defined first, because the compiler reads from the top down.
typedef works on any type

typedef doesn't only name structs. typedef unsigned int Score; makes Score another name for unsigned int. It isn't a new type, just a second name for an old one. Windows does this everywhere: in Phase 5 you'll meet DWORD, which windows.h defines as another name for an unsigned 32-bit number.
The missing semicolon

A struct definition ends with };. Forget the semicolon after the closing brace and the compiler carries on reading the next line as part of the same declaration, so MSVC's error lands on the line after the brace, often on main or the next function. When an error makes no sense, look one line up for a missing semicolon.

walk: typedef struct { ... } Player; is a blueprint. It lists the named boxes (fields) every Player has. It doesn’t create a player yet.
Fields can have different types. An array is many boxes of one type, reached by number. A struct is a few boxes of different types, reached by name.
The name after the closing brace is what typedef gives you: from now on Player is a type, like int.
Player hero; builds one real player from the blueprint. Line 11 builds a second one. They’re completely separate.
The dot reaches into one named box: hero.health is the health field of hero. You can read it or assign to it, like any int.
Only boss’s health changes. hero has its own health box.
Prints hero 100, boss 470, x 2.5. Notice hero.y is never printed: it was never set, so it holds garbage.
rungs.model: Mental model: a form with labelled boxes: x, y, health. The typedef is the blank form. Player hero; is one copy of it, and the dot says which box you mean.

check.hint: Line 15 names boss.health. Does it touch hero?
check.why: boss.health goes 500 to 470. hero.health is a separate box that was never touched, so it stays 100. Each Player built from the blueprint has its own fields.

miss.0: That would mean line 15 also lowered hero’s health. It only names boss.
miss.1: Line 15 does run: boss drops to 470.
miss.3: Both numbers are wrong: hero stays 100 and boss drops to 470.

tryit.task: Add an int field called mana to Player, then set hero’s mana to 30.

qa: Why typedef? Can I leave it out?
You can, but then you write struct Player every time. typedef lets you write just Player.
What's in a field I haven't set?
Whatever was in that memory before: garbage. Set every field before you use it, or start with = {0} or a designated initialiser so the fields you skip are 0.
Can a struct hold an array?
Yes. A field can be an int, a float, an array, even another struct. The Runner in Phase 4.5 holds its whole obstacle array this way.
How do arrays and structs fit together?

Put them together and you get the shape nearly every game runs on: Enemy enemies[MAX_ENEMIES];, one array, one loop, one struct per thing on screen. That's the next concept, Arrays of structs, and Phase 6 is built from exactly this.
rungs.bridge: You can bundle data into a struct. Next: arrays of structs, a whole wave of enemies in one array.

rungs.title: Arrays of structs
rungs.builds: Structs and the dot operator. Arrays: many values, one name, and Passing arrays to functions (Phase 3): capacity versus count.
rungs.why: Every game has more than one of something: enemies, bullets, coins. An array of structs keeps each one's data together in one box, and one loop updates them all. Phase 6 runs on exactly this shape.

parts: One array, one struct per thing

A game rarely has one enemy. Enemy enemies[MAX_ENEMIES]; is an ordinary array where every box holds a whole Enemy, fields and all. To reach one field, the index comes first and the dot second: enemies[2].health means box 2, then its health. Read it left to right and it says what it does.
Starting values with nested braces

Each enemy gets its own pair of inner braces, filled in field order:

Enemy enemies[MAX_ENEMIES] = {{0, 30}, {2, 50}, {1, 40}};

That fills three of the four boxes, and the leftover enemy is all zeros, the same rule as = {0} for an array of ints. Designated initialisers work inside the inner braces too: {.lane = 2, .health = 50}.
Capacity and count, again

This is the high-score table from Passing arrays to functions with structs in the boxes. MAX_ENEMIES is how many boxes exist. count is how many hold a real enemy right now. Loops go up to count, never to MAX_ENEMIES. Adding an enemy goes in the first unused box, and refuses when there isn't one:

int add_enemy(Enemy enemies[], int count, Enemy fresh) {
    if (count >= MAX_ENEMIES) {
        return count;
    }
    enemies[count] = fresh;
    return count + 1;
}

Call it as count = add_enemy(enemies, count, fresh);. When the wave is full the count comes back unchanged, and nothing is written past the end.
Search: an index, or -1

find_lane in the program below hands back the position of the enemy it found, so the caller can change the real one with enemies[hit]. When nothing matches it returns -1. That's safe to use as a signal because -1 can never be a real index. It's not safe to use as an index: enemies[-1] reads whatever sits in memory just before the array, with no warning. Check for -1 every time before you use the result.
A const table of enemy stats

Data that never changes while the game runs can live in a const array of structs, one row per kind of enemy:

typedef struct { int health; int speed; } EnemyStats;
const EnemyStats STATS[3] = {{30, 2}, {50, 1}, {90, 1}};

STATS[kind].health looks up the starting health for a kind, and const makes any accidental write stop the build. enum (Phase 3.75) gives the kinds names instead of 0, 1 and 2.
Beginner mistakes

• enemies.health[i] puts the index on the wrong part. The array is enemies, so the index goes straight after it.
  • Looping to MAX_ENEMIES instead of count processes the unused boxes, which hold zeros or garbage.
  • Adding without checking for a full array writes past the end, silently, like any array.

walk: A one-line typedef: every Enemy has a lane and a health.
find_lane takes the array, how many boxes are in use, and the lane to look for. const promises it only reads.
enemies[i].lane: the index picks the enemy, then the dot picks the field.
Found it: hand back its position in the array, not the enemy itself.
No enemy in that lane. -1 can never be a real index, so it's free to mean “not found”.
Nested braces: one inner pair per enemy, in field order. Box 3 isn't listed, so its lane and health are both 0.
Check for -1 before using hit as an index. enemies[-1] would read memory before the array.
This changes the real enemy in box 1: its health goes from 50 to 30.
rungs.model: Mental model: a row of lockers where each locker holds a whole form instead of one number. The index says which locker, the dot says which box on the form inside.

check.hint: Which box holds the enemy whose lane is 2? And what happens to its health before the printf?
check.why: The enemy in lane 2 sits in box 1, so find_lane returns 1. Line 19 takes 20 off its health, 50 to 30, and line 20 prints the position and the new health.

miss.1: 2 is the lane you searched for. find_lane returns the enemy's position in the array, and the lane-2 enemy is in box 1.
miss.2: Line 19 subtracts 20 from that enemy's health before the printf runs.
miss.3: enemies[1] has lane 2, so the loop finds it on its second pass and returns 1.

tryit.task: Fill the blanks: print the health of every enemy that's in use.

qa: Why return -1 and not 0 when nothing matches?
0 is a real position: the first enemy. -1 can never be an index, so it can't be mistaken for a result. NULL, at the end of this phase, is the pointer version of the same idea.
What's in enemies[3]?
Zeros. When an initialiser lists fewer enemies than the array holds, every field of the rest becomes 0. With no initialiser at all, every box is garbage.
Can I put a whole enemy into the array in one go?
Yes: enemies[count] = fresh; copies every field of fresh into that box. Structs are copied, next, shows exactly what that copy means.
Why not two arrays, lanes[] and healths[]?
That works, but every function needs both, and the day you sort or remove one and forget the other, the data no longer lines up. An array of structs keeps each enemy in one piece.
How do I remove an enemy from the middle?
The quick way: copy the last enemy in use into its box, then count--. The order changes, which rarely matters for enemies. If order matters, shift the rest down one, as the high-score table did.
rungs.bridge: You can keep a whole wave in one array. Next: what happens when you copy a struct, into a variable or into a function.

rungs.title: Structs are copied
rungs.kick: b = a · passing by value · copies
rungs.builds: Structs and the dot operator, and Arrays of structs. Scope: where a variable lives (Phase 3): an int argument is a copy, so reset() couldn't change main's score.
rungs.why: In Phase 3, reset(score) couldn't change main's score. Structs follow the same rule, and it matters more here: a damage function that works on a copy of the player does nothing at all. Seeing the problem first is what makes Passing by pointer make sense.

parts: Copying copies everything

A struct is a value, like an int. Player backup = hero; makes a second Player and copies every field into it. After that the two are separate: changing one never changes the other. Passing a struct to a function works the same way. The parameter is a fresh copy, so the function can change it all it likes and the caller's struct stays as it was. That's the rule Scope showed for an int, applied to every field at once.
Returning a struct

A function can hand a struct back, and the caller gets a copy of it:

Player make_player(int health) {
    Player p = {0};
    p.health = health;
    return p;
}

Player hero = make_player(100);

That's a tidy way to build something with sensible starting values. The starter code's player_create on the Build page works like this.
Arrays inside are copied too

If a struct has an array field, like char name[16] or int inventory[4], assigning the struct copies the whole array along with everything else. That's the one time = copies an array in C. On its own, name = other_name; still won't build, as Copying and joining strings showed.
The copy-in-a-loop bug

This looks like it moves every enemy one lane over. It moves nothing:

for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    Enemy e = enemies[i];
    e.lane += 1;
}

e is a copy of the enemy, and the copy is thrown away at the end of each pass. Write to the array itself, enemies[i].lane += 1;, or hold a pointer to the enemy, which is coming in Passing by pointer and ->.
No == for structs

if (hero == backup) doesn't build: MSVC stops with C2088 (== is illegal for a struct). Compare the fields you care about, one by one, in a small function like same_spot(a, b). C refuses partly because of padding: the compiler may leave unused bytes between fields so each one starts at a convenient address, and those bytes hold leftover junk. Two players with identical fields could still differ byte for byte.
Structs you only hold by pointer

The FILE in Saving and loading with files is a struct too, but you never make one, copy one or look inside. fopen keeps the real one and hands you a FILE *, its address. Some things should exist in exactly one place, and you're given a way to reach them instead of a copy. Pointers, next, explains that *.

walk: hurt receives a Player p: a complete copy of whatever main passes in. Every field is copied.
This lowers the copy’s health. The copy is thrown away when hurt ends.
Prints Inside hurt: 90. The function did its job, on a photocopy.
Player backup = hero; copies every field of hero into a brand new Player. From here on they’re two separate players that started out identical.
Passes a copy of hero. Nothing hurt does can reach main’s hero.
Changes backup only.
hero is still 100. backup is 1.
rungs.model: Mental model: a photocopier. Assigning a struct, or passing it to a function, photocopies the whole form. Scribbling on the copy never changes the original.

check.q: What is the second line of output?
check.hint: Which Player did hurt change? Which Player did line 17 change?
check.why: hurt only lowered its own copy, so hero stays 100. Line 17 only touched backup, which was a separate copy from line 15.

miss.1: That needs hurt to change the real hero. It only changed its copy.
miss.2: backup is a copy, not another name for hero. Setting backup can’t change hero.
miss.3: hurt can’t change hero (the copy dies), and line 17 sets backup to 1.

tryit.task: Copy a into b, then set only b’s health to 5.

qa: So how does a function change the real player?
By being given the player's address instead of a copy. That's a pointer: Pointers: & and * and then Passing by pointer and ->.
Is copying a big struct slow?
It copies every byte. For a small struct it's nothing. For a big one, passing an address is cheaper too, which is a second reason games pass pointers.
Why did insert_score change my real array in Phase 3?
Arrays are the exception: passing an array hands over where it lives, not a copy. A struct has no such shortcut, so it's copied. Pointers and arrays, later in this phase, shows why.
Does b = a behave the same in GDScript?
No. In GDScript objects are references, so b = a gives two names for one object and setting b.health changes a.health too. In C a struct is a value, so you get two separate players.
rungs.bridge: You’ve seen the problem: a copy can’t change the original. Next: pointers, a way to hold where something lives.

rungs.title: Pointers: & and *
rungs.builds: Reading input with scanf (Phase 2): scanf(&x) handed scanf the address of x. Saving and loading with files (Phase 3): the FILE * you were told to ignore. Structs are copied: a copy can't change the original.
rungs.why: A pointer is a variable that holds where something lives instead of the thing itself. Hand a function that address and it can reach back and change the original. Every game function that updates the player works this way.

parts: Memory is numbered bytes

Your program's memory is one long row of bytes, and every byte has a number: its address. An int takes 4 bytes, and its address is the number of the first one. &score gives you that number. A pointer is a variable whose job is to hold one. When p holds score's address, we say p points at score.
Why a pointer has a type

An address only says where something starts. The type says what's there: int* p means “at this address there's an int”, so *p reads 4 bytes as a whole number. A float* would read 4 bytes as a decimal, and a Player* a whole Player. That's why you can't freely mix them. Point an int* at a float and MSVC warns, because the bytes would be read the wrong way.
Copy the pointer, or what it points at?

Two lines that look alike do different jobs:

int lives = 3, shield = 1;
int* p = &lives;
int* q = &shield;

q = p;     /* q now points at lives too */
*q = *p;   /* copies the value lives holds into wherever q points */

q = p copies the address: now there are two notes with the same house on them, and shield is no longer reachable through q. *q = *p copies the int from one box to the other, and both pointers stay where they were.
A pointer starts as garbage

Like any local variable, int* p; holds leftover junk until you set it, and junk in a pointer is a random address. *p = 5; would write 5 somewhere nobody chose. Give a pointer a real address the moment you make it, or NULL if there isn't one yet (NULL is the last concept in this phase).

MSVC catches the simple case with C4700, the same uninitialised-variable warning you met in Phase 2, and /WX stops the build.
The int* a, b trap
int* a, b; looks like two pointers. It's one pointer and one plain int: the * belongs to the name next to it, not to the type. That's why this course declares one pointer per line.
Printing an address

printf("%p\n", (void*)p); prints the address p holds. On x64 MSVC shows 16 hex digits with no 0x in front, like 000000A3F9D6FBA0, because a 64-bit address is 8 bytes. The number changes from run to run, so never write code that depends on its value. The (void*) cast is what %p officially expects. MSVC doesn't insist, but other compilers do.

walk: An ordinary int. Somewhere in memory there’s a box holding 10, and that box has an address.
&score means “the address of score”: the same & you gave scanf. int* p declares a variable that holds the address of an int. Now p points at score.
copy gets the value 10. It’s a separate box, so it has nothing to do with score from now on.
*p means “go to the address in p and use what’s there”. This line writes 50 into score’s box.
score changed, though it was never named on line 8. copy is still 10.
*p reads the same box, so it prints 50. Two names for one box: score, and *p.
rungs.model: Mental model: a note with a house address on it. &score writes the address down. p is the note. *p means walk to that address and open the front door.

check.q: What is the first line of output?
check.hint: *p = 50 writes into score’s box. Does copy share that box?
check.why: p holds score’s address, so *p = 50 changes score to 50. copy took the value 10 on line 6, before the change, and lives in its own box.

miss.0: Line 8 does run: it changes score through the pointer.
miss.1: copy is a separate box that got its value earlier. It doesn’t follow score.
miss.2: Backwards: score is the one that changes, through p.

tryit.task: Make p point at lives, then set lives to 3 through p.

qa: The * appears in two places. Is it the same thing?
Related but different jobs. In a declaration (int* p) it means “p is a pointer”. In an expression (*p = 50) it means “go to the address”. & is the reverse: “give me the address”.
Is int *p different from int* p?
No, the compiler treats them the same. This roadmap writes int* p, and the FILE *f from Phase 3 is the same idea written the other way. Either way, declare one pointer per line.
What does a pointer actually print as?
A long hex number like 000000A1B2EFF7A4 (16 digits, because a 64-bit address is 8 bytes). Use %p to print one. You'll also see them in the debugger's Watch window in The debugger (Phase 3.75).
GDScript has no pointers. Why does C make me deal with them?

GDScript has something similar, it just hides it: objects are passed by reference, which works much like a pointer with the asterisk filed off. C makes you choose between copying a whole struct every frame and handing over one address.
rungs.bridge: You can hold an address and follow it. Next: handing a function an address, and the -> shortcut for structs.

rungs.title: Passing by pointer and ->
rungs.builds: Structs are copied and Pointers: & and *: a copy can't change the original, but an address can. Scope: where a variable lives (Phase 3), and its reset() that didn't work.
rungs.why: Time to fix Phase 3’s reset problem. If a function takes a pointer, the caller passes an address with &, and the function reaches back through it. This is why player_move takes a Player* and not a Player.

parts: Hand over the address

A function gets copies of its arguments, as Scope and Structs are copied showed. The way round that is to pass an address. The parameter is a pointer, void reset(int* score), and the caller passes an address with &: reset(&hero.score);. Inside, *score = 0; follows the address and writes into the caller's box. The pointer itself is still a copy, but a copy of an address leads to the same place as the original.
A field through a pointer: (*p).health, then ->

With Player* p, *p is the whole Player that p points at, so (*p).health is its health field. The brackets matter. The dot is applied before the *, so *p.health means *(p.health): take the health field of p, then follow it. p isn't a struct, so that doesn't build.

Writing (*p). every time gets old, so C has a shorthand: p->health means exactly (*p).health. The rule is short. Holding the struct itself? Use the dot: hero.health. Holding its address? Use the arrow: p->health.

Write p.health on a pointer and MSVC stops with C2231. Its message says the left side points to a struct and tells you to use ->.
Output parameters: returning more than one thing

return hands back one value. When a function has two answers, the caller passes addresses for the function to fill:

void split_frames(int frames, int* secs, int* left) {
    *secs = frames / 60;
    *left = frames % 60;
}

int secs = 0, left = 0;
split_frames(150, &secs, &left);   /* 2 and 30 */

scanf has worked this way since Phase 2. That's why it needed &guess: it was filling your variable through its address.
Forgetting the &

Call reset(hero.score) when reset wants an int* and you've passed the number 99 where an address belongs. MSVC catches it with C4047 (the argument “differs in levels of indirection”: an int where an int* was expected), and /WX stops the build. Without that check the function would treat 99 as an address and write there. The rule to remember: if the parameter has a *, the argument needs an address, which usually means an & in front of a variable.
Changing one enemy in an array

The same move works on one element of an array of structs. &enemies[i] is the address of box i, so a function that takes an Enemy* can change that enemy and no other:

void damage_enemy(Enemy* e, int amount) {
    e->health -= amount;
}

damage_enemy(&enemies[2], 40);

Inside, it's the arrow as usual. Compare this with the copy-in-a-loop bug from Structs are copied: there the loop changed a copy, here the function holds the real enemy's address.
const Player*: look, don't touch

Passing a pointer is cheap even for a big struct, so functions that only read a Player take one too. Mark them with const:

void print_player(const Player* p) {
    printf("health %d\n", p->health);
}

Any line inside that writes through p now stops the build. It's the same promise as a const array parameter in Passing arrays to functions: anyone reading the first line knows print_player only looks.
Never return the address of a local

A local variable dies when its function returns, so a pointer to it points at a box that's gone:

int* best_score(void) {
    int best = 900;
    return &best;
}

The caller gets an address that the next function call will reuse for something else. This is a dangling pointer. It may even print 900 once, which makes it worse.

MSVC warns C4172 (returning address of local variable) and /WX stops the build. Return the value itself, or have the caller pass in a pointer to fill.

walk: The parameter is int* score: a pointer. The function receives an address, not a copy of the number.
Goes to that address and writes 0. This is the reset() that Phase 3 couldn’t write.
Player* p: heal gets the address of a Player, so it works on the real one.
p->health is shorthand for (*p).health: follow the pointer, then take the health field. With a pointer, use the arrow.
The caller passes &hero.score: the address of that one field.
&hero is the address of the whole Player. heal follows it and changes the real hero.
Prints health 85, score 0. Both changes stuck.
rungs.model: Mental model: giving someone your address instead of a photocopy of your house plans. They can walk in and move the furniture. Dot when you hold the thing (hero.health), arrow when you hold its address (p->health).

check.q: On line 13 you write p.health instead of p->health. What happens?
check.hint: The dot works on a struct you hold. What kind of thing is p?
check.why: p is a Player*, an address, not a Player. The dot only works on a struct itself, so the compiler refuses. Pointer means arrow; actual struct means dot.

miss.0: They’re not interchangeable. The dot needs a struct, the arrow needs a pointer to one.
miss.2: It never gets that far: the compiler won’t accept the dot on a pointer at all.
miss.3: That never runs. The compiler rejects the line before the program exists.

tryit.task: Write damage so it lowers the real player’s health.

qa: Where do I put the & when I call?
On the variable you want changed: heal(&hero, 25). If the parameter is a pointer, the caller passes an address. Leave the & off and MSVC stops the build with C4047.
Can I still just use (*p).health?
Yes, it means exactly the same thing. The arrow is the shorthand everyone uses.
Does this fix Phase 3's array behaviour too?
It explains half of it. An array's name already acts like the address of its first box, which is why insert_score changed your real array all along. Pointers and arrays, next, finishes the story.
When do I use the arrow and when the dot?

Holding a pointer? Use the arrow: p->health. Holding the actual struct? Use the dot: player.health. With an array of structs, enemies[i] is a struct, so it's enemies[i].health, and &enemies[i] is the address you'd pass to a function.
rungs.bridge: You can hand a function the real thing. Next: pointers and arrays, and why Phase 3's array parameters changed the caller's array.

rungs.title: Pointers and arrays
rungs.kick: p + 1 · a[i] is *(a + i) · int a[] is int* a · const char*
rungs.builds: Pointers: & and *, and Passing by pointer and ->. Passing arrays to functions (Phase 3), which promised this explanation. Strings and the '\0' at the end (Phase 3).
rungs.why: In Phase 3 a function could change your real array, and sizeof inside it gave the wrong answer. Both come from one rule: an array's name turns into a pointer to its first element. Once you see that, array parameters, string literals and pointer loops in other people's code all make sense.

parts: Pointers can step through an array

Point p at an element, int* p = &hits[1];, and p + 1 is the address of the next element, hits[2]. It isn't the next byte. C scales the step by the type: for an int it moves 4 bytes, for a double 8, for a Player the size of a whole Player. You never do that maths yourself. There are three things you can do:

  • Add a whole number: p + 2 is two elements further on, and p++ moves p one along.
  • Subtract a whole number: p - 1 is one element back.
  • Subtract two pointers into the same array: &hits[3] - &hits[1] is 2, how many elements apart they are.

Comparing with < works too, as long as both point into the same array.
One past the end

For a 4-element array, hits + 4 is a legal address to make and compare against, which is exactly what a loop's stopping test needs: p < hits + count. It's one past the last element, and you must never read or write through it. Anything further out, or anything before hits[0], isn't even legal to make. As with array indexes, nothing warns you: going too far just reads or writes someone else's memory.
a[i] is *(a + i)

When you use an array's name in an expression, C quietly turns it into a pointer to element 0. People call this array decay. Indexing is pointer arithmetic underneath: hits[3] means *(hits + 3), step three ints along from the start and read what's there. That's also why indexes start at 0: element 0 is zero steps from the start.

The name itself isn't a variable you can move, though. hits = other; and hits++ both stop the build, just like assigning a string with = did.
Why array parameters change the caller's array

This finishes what Passing arrays to functions started in Phase 3. In a parameter list, int scores[] really means int* scores, and the call add_bonus(scores, count, 5) passes the address of scores[0]. So:

  • No copy is made: the function writes into the caller's boxes through that address.
  • sizeof(scores) inside gives 8, the size of a pointer on x64.
  • A number inside the brackets is thrown away, because a pointer has no length.

const int scores[] is the same as const int* scores, which is how sum_hits below is written.
A pointer is not an array

You can index a pointer, p[1], and do arithmetic on an array name, so they're easy to mix up. They aren't the same thing. An array owns its boxes: sizeof(hits) is 16, four ints of 4 bytes. A pointer owns nothing but one address: sizeof(p) is 8 on x64, whatever it points at. You can aim a pointer somewhere else whenever you like. An array stays where it was made.
Text in quotes: const char*

const char* name = "Sam"; points at text the program stores for you, often in memory you're not allowed to change. The const makes the compiler refuse name[0] = 'P';, which would otherwise build and then crash or quietly do nothing. If you need text you can change, make your own copy with char name[] = "Sam";. Fixed text is where const char* shines, for example a field in a table of enemy kinds: {"Slime", 30}.
MSVC notes

MSVC doesn't warn about sizeof on an array parameter, or about a pointer stepping past the end of an array. Both build cleanly at /W4. Pass the count, and keep loop tests in the p < start + count shape.

*p reads the element p is on right now.
p holds the address of hits[1], which holds 5.
p + 2 is two ints further on, hits[3]. Prints 5 7.
hits[3] and *(hits + 3) are the same thing: the name becomes a pointer to element 0, then step three along.
sizeof(hits) is 16: the whole array, four 4-byte ints. sizeof(p) is 8: one address on x64.
const char* points at the text "Sam", stored by the program. const stops you writing to it.

qa: So is an array's name a pointer?
No. It turns into one when you use it in most expressions. sizeof(hits) is the main exception: there it still means the whole array, which is why sizeof gives 16 in main and 8 inside a function.
Should I loop with pointers or with [i]?

Either. With optimisation on, they usually compile to the same thing. This course uses [i] most of the time because it reads more clearly. You still need to read pointer loops, because other people's code is full of them.
What does *p++ do?
It reads the value p points at, then moves p one along. The ++ belongs to p, not to the value. To add one to the value, write (*p)++.
Why not just write char* name = "Sam"?
C allows it, but it's a trap: the text may live in read-only memory, so writing to it can crash, and nothing stops you trying. const char* turns that mistake into a build error.

rungs.title: NULL
rungs.builds: Passing by pointer and ->: functions that take a Player*. Arrays of structs: returning -1 for “not found”. Saving and loading with files (Phase 3): fopen returns NULL when a file can't be opened.
rungs.why: A pointer can hold “no address at all”: NULL. Following it is undefined behaviour, and on Windows that almost always means a crash. Functions use NULL to say “I couldn’t give you one”, like fopen did in Phase 3, so you check before you follow a pointer.

parts: A pointer to nothing
NULL is a pointer value that means “no address”. It's how a function says “I couldn't give you one”. fopen returns NULL when the file won't open, and your own functions can do the same.
Returning NULL from a search

Arrays of structs searched for an enemy and returned its index, or -1. The pointer version returns the enemy's address, or NULL:

Enemy* find_enemy(Enemy enemies[], int count, int lane) {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        if (enemies[i].lane == lane) {
            return &enemies[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

The caller checks, then uses the arrow: Enemy* e = find_enemy(enemies, count, 2); and if (e != NULL) { e->health -= 20; }. Returning &enemies[i] is fine where returning the address of a local wasn't, because the array belongs to the caller and is still there after find_enemy returns.
if (p) and if (!p)

In a test, NULL counts as false and every real address counts as true. So if (e) means “if there is an enemy” and if (!f) means “if there's no file”. They do the same job as comparing with NULL. Pick one style and stick to it; this course writes == NULL because it reads plainly.
NULL is the only bad pointer you can test for

A pointer can go bad in other ways:

  • Garbage: never set, so it holds a random address.
  • Dangling: it pointed at something that has ended, like a local from a function that returned.
  • Out of bounds: stepped past the end of its array.

All three look like ordinary addresses, and there's no test that tells them apart from a good one. That's why the habit matters: give every pointer a real address or NULL the moment you make it, and don't keep pointers to things that end.
Where NULL comes from

NULL is defined in the standard headers, such as stddef.h, stdio.h, string.h and stdlib.h. Use it with none of them included and MSVC reports it as undeclared (C2065). And NULL is not '\0'. Both are zero, but NULL is a pointer and '\0' is the character that ends a string, so name[i] == NULL is the wrong test. Newer code may use C23's nullptr; under MSVC's C17 mode, write NULL.
The crash is the good outcome

Following NULL is undefined behaviour, but on Windows it nearly always stops the program on the spot with an access violation, because address zero is never part of your program's memory. In the terminal the program just ends, and echo %ERRORLEVEL% shows -1073741819, Windows' code for an access violation. That sounds bad, but it's the best kind of bug: loud, at the exact line. The debugger (Phase 3.75) stops right on that line. A garbage pointer can instead change some other variable and say nothing.

walk: The guard. NULL is a pointer that points at nothing. Check for it before using the pointer.

Only reached when p is a real address.

Now target holds hero’s address.
This time the check passes, so hero heals to 60.
The same pattern from Phase 3. FILE * is a pointer too, and fopen returns NULL when it can’t open the file.

qa: Why does NULL crash instead of doing nothing?
Address zero is never part of your program's memory, so the operating system stops you the moment you touch it. That's louder than silent wrong answers.
Should every pointer be checked?
Check the ones that can legitimately be NULL: fopen results, a search that found nothing. A pointer you got from &hero can never be NULL.
Is NULL the same as 0?
It compares equal to 0, and on Windows it really is address zero. Write NULL when you mean a pointer, so the code says what you mean.
Can I check for a dangling pointer?

No. It holds a real-looking address, and nothing about it says the thing it pointed at has gone. The fix is to not create one: never return the address of a local, and set a pointer to NULL when what it pointed at is finished.
